topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations

outline.topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations

sections.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Transformation Perspective
sections.content: Recall that a matrix represents a function: it takes a vector 'v' as input and outputs a transformed vector 'w' (w = Av). Visualize this as a grid shift: a matrix A stretches or rotates the entire coordinate plane.
sections.example: Visualizing a 2x2 matrix as a transformation grid that tilts a unit square.

sections.title: The Concept of Function Composition
sections.content: Define composition: If we apply transformation B first, then transformation A, the result is a new 'combined' transformation. We denote this as A(B(v)). The goal is to find a single matrix C such that C = AB.
sections.example: A robotic arm: Matrix B rotates the arm base, and Matrix A extends the reach. Applying them sequentially is equivalent to a single 'combined' reach-and-rotate matrix C.

sections.title: Visualizing the Chain Reaction
sections.content: Focus on the basis vectors (i = [1, 0] and j = [0, 1]). First, B moves i and j to new positions B(i) and B(j). Then, A moves those new vectors again. The final positions of i and j determine the columns of the new matrix C.
sections.example: Animation: Use a 'Grid Monster'. It first stretches the grid (B), then the result is rotated by the next transformation (A). The combined grid movement is the matrix product AB.

sections.title: Deriving the Rule: Why 'Row by Column'?
sections.content: Explain that matrix multiplication is not commutative (AB ≠ BA). It is simply the bookkeeping method to track where the basis vectors end up after two successive mappings.
sections.example: A 2D character (e.g., a cat icon) on a screen: Matrix B scales it, Matrix A reflects it. Demonstrating that flipping then scaling (AB) results in a different final pose than scaling then flipping (BA).

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Reiterate that matrix multiplication is a geometric 'shortcut'. Instead of applying two functions, we multiply the matrices once to capture the entire composite movement of the space.
sections.example: A shortcut for computer graphics engines: Pre-calculating a single 'Combined Matrix' for character movement instead of calculating every frame step-by-step.

storyboard.title: The Concept of Function Composition
lecture_lines: Composition means applying one transformation after another.
We apply B first, then A to result C.
We want a single matrix C for AB.
Robotic arm rotates then extends its reach.
This sequence equals a combined transformation matrix.

storyboard.title: Visualizing the Chain Reaction
lecture_lines: Track the basis vectors i and j.
B moves basis vectors to new positions.
A then moves those results again.
Final positions define the columns of matrix C.
This chain is the matrix product AB.

storyboard.title: Deriving the Rule: Why 'Row by Column'?
lecture_lines: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so AB does not equal BA.
It tracks where basis vectors end up after two mappings.
Scaling then flipping differs from flipping then scaling.

storyboard.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: Matrix multiplication is a geometric shortcut.
Multiply matrices once to capture the full movement.
Compute a single matrix for efficient composite transformations.
